extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP counsel, patent prosecutors, and law students studying §101 case law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-based criteria for evaluating whether asserted patent claims are directed to an abstract idea and whether they supply an inventive concept under the Alice/Mayo framework. Compiles district-court holdings illustrating factors courts treat as indicative of eligibility or ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim is "directed to an abstract idea" (Alice step 1). Courts identify abstract ideas in examples such as collecting/gathering data, analyzing data, storing results, matching identifiers to retrieve information, filtering content, routing calls, tailoring scripts, or other fundamental economic or conventional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from cases: claims were held directed to abstract ideas where they covered "gathering information and translating it between two or more incompatible formats," "filtering content," "allowing a party to select between voice call and electronic chat," "tailoring a script to a particular customer," or "collecting, transmitting, and displaying location information." If a claim is characterized as an abstract idea, the analysis proceeds to whether it contains an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains an inventive concept (Alice step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim supplies an "inventive concept" that transforms an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., reciting something significantly more than the abstract idea itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts found inventive concept where claims: recited components "in a specific manner for a specifically configured path," recited a "specific arrangement of components and a very specific implementation and structure of the executable program code," recited a "new kind of virus protection," or recited limitations that "improve the functioning of a computer" or constitute a "technical improvement over prior art ways." Courts also note that the fact a claim "adds little to the prior art ... does not mean that the claim lacks an inventive concept vis-à-vis an abstract idea."

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve computer or technological functioning are more likely eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to or effectuate an improvement in computer/information technology (not merely using a computer as a tool) are treated as non-abstract or as providing an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: claims that "improve the functioning of [a] computer due to 'user-configured business rules and configurable/application links,'" claims that make synchronization faster, reduce bandwidth/storage, enable synchronization across formats, improve cellular networking, enhance data compression or transmission efficiency, or "improve an existing technological process." Courts repeatedly accept eligibility where the claim solves a problem "rooted in computer technology."

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting specific physical components or tangible limitations supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that include concrete physical devices, apparatus elements, or steps requiring physical action (i.e., "activity outside of one's mind") are less likely to be characterized as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases treated claims as non-abstract where they recited a "piece of exercise equipment," "dispatch and mobile unit," "unmanned aerial vehicles," a "tangible resumption of an interrupted file download," a "new and useful arrangement" of hardware for haptic/vibrotactile devices, or where steps like "detecting the presence of a person at a door, sending a video, and speaking" were required. Courts emphasize physical or apparatus limitations ("specialized equipment" or "physical limitations") as favoring eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific arrangement or unconventional combination of known components can supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that claim a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement or combination of known pieces can provide the inventive concept needed for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: courts credited claims that recited "a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces," or recited an "unconventional arrangement" that avoided prior-art linkage practices (e.g., add/remove persons via buddy list). Such recitations may be treated as an inventive concept even where individual components are conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of concrete implementation details (software/structure) supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite concrete implementation details (e.g., the "specific implementation and structure of the executable program code") rather than high-level functional results are more likely to be found to contain an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases found eligibility where claims described "a specific arrangement of components and a very specific implementation and structure of the executable program code," or "describe[d] how a solution will be implemented that addresses a business challenge particular to the Internet." The level of claimed specificity and structure is a recurring factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems unique to computer/technical world weigh toward eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention addresses a problem that exists only in the technical realm (e.g., Internet, cellular networks, IMS architectures, distinguishing humans from computers), courts view the claim as more likely to be non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holdings: claims solving issues "created by the design of cellular networks," "a problem that currently exists only within the technical world" (e.g., CAPTCHA), or problems specific to IMS architectures or online gaming have been held not to be directed to abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or algorithms are suspect but can be eligible when improving technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to mathematical formulas or algorithms are often characterized as abstract, but eligibility can be found where the mathematical element is applied to effect a technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: some MPEG decoder claims were "directed to no more than a mathematical formula," but the court nonetheless found they did "attempt to improve a technological issue" and thus did not lack an inventive concept. Courts look for application of math/algorithms to solve a technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely collect/analyze/store information tend to be abstract absent inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic claims that amount to collecting data, analyzing it for characteristics, and storing results are frequently treated as abstract ideas unless the claim includes a qualifying inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual example: claims described as the abstract idea of "gathering data, analyzing that data for certain characteristics, and storing the results of that analysis" were held ineligible when no inventive concept was present. Courts require more than data handling in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that limit themselves to a particular technological environment or concrete structure can show inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting claims to a particular technological environment (e.g., cellular communications) or to a particular concrete device/structure can support a finding of inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims limited to "cellular communications and the concrete structure of a mobile device," claims reciting "the inclusion of a specific set of 16 cyclic shift intervals," or reciting a dispatch/mobile unit were treated as having inventive concept by virtue of their concrete technological framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of defendant to show elements are 'well‑understood, routine, conventional' undermines finding of no inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts treat evidence about whether claimed limitations are merely well-understood, routine, and conventional as dispositive; absent such evidence, a challenge under step two may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a court denied summary judgment where defendants "failed to submit any evidence that the claims recited 'well‑understood, routine or conventional activities.'" Thus the party attacking eligibility bears an evidentiary burden on conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that can be performed entirely by mental steps are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed steps are such that they could be performed entirely in the human mind or via pen-and-paper, courts are likely to characterize the claim as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases flagged claims as abstract where the asserted invention boiled down to mental processes or could be performed by a person without specialized hardware. Conversely, courts note that adding mere data or information (without technical implementation) may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting 'how' a solution is implemented (not just the result) favors eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that explain 'how' a claimed result is achieved — i.e., specific processes, links, business rules, or component interactions — are more likely to survive §101 scrutiny than claims that assert only an outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, claims that "specif[y] how a solution will be implemented that addresses a business challenge particular to the Internet" or recite "user-configured business rules and configurable/application links" were treated as improving computer functioning and thus non-abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims solving scaling or architecture-specific networking problems are more likely eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that propose a novel network structure or approach to transmit/distribute data as the number of participants scales or that address architecture-specific issues (e.g., IMS) are seen as addressing technical problems and not mere abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases found eligibility where claims covered "an innovative network structure for the distribution of data as the number of participants in a computer network is scaled," or where claims solved a "particular technical problem that only existed in wireless communication networks operating under an IMS architecture."

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that provide tangible improvements to device capabilities are eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effect tangible changes in device operation or provide capabilities beyond traditional systems (e.g., controlling device configurations, enabling new detection modalities) support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: volume control claims providing capabilities beyond hardwired systems, POS terminal improvements, or haptic devices notifying users via vibration were held non-abstract because the claims improved device functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to particular data formats, storage/synchronization methods, or bandwidth optimizations supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that specify particular data-format handling, synchronization methods across formats, or bandwidth/storage optimizations can be treated as technological improvements rather than abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: claims reciting faster synchronization, reducing bandwidth and storage, enabling synchronization without physical connection, and lossless compression/decompression tied to storage/retrieval were found to improve computer/data-handling technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of specialized codes, intervals, or multi-code procedures can indicate specificity/non‑abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require particular codes, numerous access codes, or specific interval sets are treated as reciting specialized procedures rather than generic abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims using "four different access codes," a "specific set of 16 cyclic shift intervals," or similar particularized procedural limitations were relied upon by courts to conclude the claims recited specialized procedures and thus were not merely abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/overbroad claim drafting favors ineligibility when lacking technical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims drafted as broad functional results (e.g., "providing directions") without technical detail or concrete implementation are vulnerable to being characterized as abstract and ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases courts found claims covering "providing directions in a natural language" or other high-level functionality to be non-abstract only where the claim also recited particular technical implementations; otherwise broad functional language alone is risky.
